title: Usability Tests vs. Concept Tests
intro: Moderated usability testing comes from behavioural science: give real users a real goal and watch what they do. Many teams say “we did a usability test” when they actually asked people what they thought.

learn.title: Behaviour, not opinion
learn.text:
A usability test shows **what real users do** when faced with a real goal. That is still the gold standard.

A concept test asks for reactions: “What do you think this button does?” “Would you use something like this?”

“Real intuitiveness is not a feeling; it is a measurable outcome.”

try.q: In a session you asked “Would you use something like this?” and wrote down the answers. What did you run?
options: A concept test
A usability test
A cognitive walkthrough
A heuristic evaluation
try.explain: Collecting opinions about a design is concept testing, whatever the meeting was called.

learn.title: Write tasks as intent
learn.text:
Bad instructions describe the interface:
❌ “Click the download button.”
❌ “Find the profile page and update your settings.”

Good instructions state the intent:
✅ “You want to keep a copy of this for your records.”
✅ “You need to change something about how the system notifies you.”

try.q: Which task is written as intent?
options: You want to keep a copy of this for your records.
Click the download button in the toolbar.
Open the File menu and choose Export as PDF.
Find the profile page and update your notification settings.
try.explain: It gives a goal and leaves the route open, so you learn whether the interface supports it.

learn.title: When concept testing fits
learn.text:
Concept testing has a place: **early-stage ideas**, when you need to know if the general direction makes sense.

But most of the time teams use it where a usability test would give much better data: when there is something users could interact with.

try.q: When is a concept test the reasonable choice?
options: Early ideas, to check the general direction
Validating a finished redesign shortly before launch
Finding friction in an existing checkout
Measuring whether a flow is intuitive
try.explain: Once users can interact with something, test behaviour instead.

test.q: Where does moderated usability testing come from?
options: Behavioural science
Agile product rituals
Marketing focus groups
Visual design critique
test.explain: It was built by researchers such as Gould, Lewis, Nielsen and Virzi who studied what people did, not what they said.

test.q: Which is a sign you ran a concept test, not a usability test?
options: You gathered quotes instead of observing actions
Participants failed several of the tasks you had prepared
The prototype was built in low fidelity
A moderator was present in the session
test.explain: Other signs: asking how they'd imagine it working, or testing a design nobody interacts with.

test.q: What should you do before writing usability test tasks?
options: Work out what people are actually trying to do
Decide which screens look most finished
Ask stakeholders which features they most want to show off
Write the report template for the findings
test.explain: Start with a task analysis, not the UI.

test.q: What is wrong with “Find the profile page and update your settings”?
options: It describes the interface, not the user's intent
It is too long for most participants to remember accurately
It tests two different pages at once
It doesn't include a time limit
test.explain: It hands the route to the participant, so you only test instruction-following.

test.q: How does Calabro define real intuitiveness?
options: A measurable outcome
A feeling users report
A sign of clean visual design
Something experts can judge by eye
test.explain: “Real intuitiveness is not a feeling; it is a measurable outcome.”
